newsitem.title: UK: Two explosions hit Belfast police station.
newsitem.headline: Two explosions hit Belfast police station.

text.p: Northern Ireland police on Monday reported two explosions at a police station in Belfast.
The blasts were at the Mount Pottinger police station in the Short Strand area of the city.
Police had no immediate reports of any injuries, although residents said a woman had been taken away in an ambulance, possibly suffering from shock.
"We have first reports of two explosions shortly after 7 a.m. in the vicinity of Mount Pottinger police station," a police spokesman said.
Houses around the police station were being evacuated, a police spokesman added. Army bomb disposal experts had been called in case there were any further unexploded bombs.
Local people said the blast had shattered windows in nearby houses.
The latest explosions come as the Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, has directed a series of attacks against police stations and mobile patrols.

Northern Ireland's police chief, Ronnie Flanagan, said on Sunday that IRA guerrillas appeared determined to kill members of his force in a rapidly escalating 1997 campaign which has raised fears of a return to total sectarian warfare.
Two police officers and a woman motorist had a narrow escape at the weekend when two horizontal mortars were fired at a police patrol near Downpatrick, southeast of Belfast.

The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year by bombing targets in Britain and a British army base in Germany in protest at the failure of its political wing, Sinn Fein, to win a seat at multi-party peace talks in Belfast.
No-one has been killed in Northern Ireland since the IRA returned to war in the province itself by bombing Britain's army base outside Belfast last October, killing one soldier.

But security forces fear that it is only a matter of time before the IRA kills a member of the 18,000-strong police force and its Protestant Loyalist adversaries respond by returning to tit-for-tat revenge violence.
The Ulster Freedom Fighters, one outlawed Loyalist group, said last month that it would end its truce if the IRA killed anyone and police say they are taking the threat seriously.
Loyalists, who want Northern Ireland to remain British, called a truce in October 1994.
